summary: Discusses where Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is suitable for traffic engineering in IP networks. It covers deployment considerations in operational networks and points out the limits of the MPLS approach.

plainLanguage.summary: Traffic engineering means steering cars so no road is jammed. This document says when using MPLS labels to steer internet traffic works well and when it does not.

subtitle: When and how to use labeled paths to optimize network traffic flow

tldr.problem: IP networks using shortest-path routing can become congested on certain links while other paths sit underutilized, wasting capacity and reducing performance.
tldr.mechanism: MPLS Traffic Engineering uses labeled switched paths (LSP-tunnels) to forward traffic over chosen routes that bypass congested links, giving operators fine-grained control over traffic placement independent of shortest-path calculations.
tldr.outcome: Networks can better distribute traffic across available capacity, but MPLS TE introduces operational complexity, requires careful capacity planning, and is not a substitute for proper network sizing.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: MPLS traffic engineering in service provider networks

today: RFC 3346 remains an informational resource on MPLS traffic engineering applicability. MPLS TE is widely deployed in service provider networks, though many of the operational challenges the RFC describes—particularly around network management and the resource investment required—continue to be relevant concerns.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
This RFC discusses when and how Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is suitable for traffic engineering in IP networks. Traffic engineering means mapping traffic flows onto the network topology in the most effective way to achieve operational goals.

MPLS adds the ability to create explicitly routed paths (called LSP-tunnels) that ignore the shortest-path routes chosen by standard Interior Gateway Protocols (IGPs) like OSPF and IS-IS. This gives network operators significant flexibility in directing traffic and implementing policies to optimize network performance.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS is a way to tell packets which path to take through the network instead of always taking the shortest path. This helps prevent traffic jams on certain links.

sections.title: Why Traffic Engineering Matters
sections.content:
ISPs and large networks often find that certain links become congested while other parts of the network have spare capacity. Traditional IP routing always chooses the shortest path, which can lead to poor utilization of the network's overall capacity.

MPLS traffic engineering solves this by allowing operators to explicitly route traffic away from congested links onto less congested paths. An operator can create an LSP between two nodes that are known to send traffic through a bottleneck, and route that LSP through a separate path to redirect some traffic away from the congestion.
sections.plainLanguage: When the main road is packed but side roads are empty, traffic engineering lets you send some cars down the side roads instead.

sections.title: Key Applications and Techniques
sections.content:
The RFC identifies several scenarios where MPLS traffic engineering provides value. Networks with parallel links between nodes—such as multiple transoceanic circuits or bandwidth-constrained cities—can use MPLS to distribute traffic across those links more evenly than standard routing would.

Another powerful use of MPLS is affinities: arbitrary attributes applied to links that let operators group links logically and implement routing policies. For example, a global provider might use affinities to keep continental traffic within a continent and force inter-regional traffic to take dedicated circuits. Networks with mixed link capacities (OC-12, OC-48, OC-192) can use affinities to force certain traffic types to use only certain capacity levels.

After a network failure, MPLS TE can also re-optimize the paths of surviving LSPs to improve performance over the remaining topology, complementing fast-reroute mechanisms that reduce immediate packet loss.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS lets network operators set rules like 'keep this type of traffic on fast links' or 'use multiple roads for this big flow' to make the best use of the network.

sections.title: Implementation and Operational Considerations
sections.content:
Deploying MPLS TE in production networks requires careful attention to many factors. Operators must decide how many LSP-tunnels to create, as too few means insufficient control over traffic but too many increases operational complexity. A hierarchical network approach (core and edge networks) can help manage scalability while keeping the core heavily traffic-engineered.

Bandwidth allocation for each LSP must be managed carefully. Operators should base LSP bandwidth on measured traffic statistics and monitor flows constantly for unusual behavior. Over-subscription of LSP capacity must be accounted for to handle flows that occasionally exceed their normal limits.

Network management is critical but challenging. Early adopters of MPLS often built custom in-house management systems because commercial Network Management Systems (NMS) with proper MPLS support were unavailable. The RFC emphasizes that proper LSP bandwidth modeling and stability monitoring of LSP transitions are essential for maintaining network performance.
sections.plainLanguage: Running MPLS Traffic Engineering means constantly watching how much traffic each labeled path carries, adjusting the paths when needed, and having good tools to see what's happening—all of which is hard work.

sections.title: Limitations and Reality Checks
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes several important limitations of MPLS TE. Significant engineering and testing resources are required to understand how MPLS works and to identify problems with vendor implementations. Configuration management can consume considerable resources, and manual tweaks to router configurations are difficult to track.

Architectural choices can create scalability problems, especially designs that create full meshes of LSPs. The number of LSPs grows as O(N^2) where N is the number of edge nodes, which can overwhelm router implementations and protocol stability.

MPLS TE is a connection-oriented approach, unlike traditional connectionless IP routing, which complicates operational analysis. Forwarding state mismatches in MPLS result in dropped packets, whereas connectionless routing would loop or misdirect packets.

Most importantly, MPLS TE is not a substitute for proper capacity planning and network dimensioning. It cannot solve the fundamental problem of insufficient capacity. While TE can temporarily accommodate more traffic on a given topology during periods of growth, it cannot achieve impossible mappings of traffic onto topologies. Networks must be properly sized or congestion will occur regardless of what traffic engineering techniques are applied.
sections.plainLanguage: MPLS takes a lot of work to set up and manage. It can help with congestion, but if you don't buy enough cables and routers, traffic will still jam no matter what.
